# CB RULES for the look-finisher (GENERATED 2026-11-15 by tools/slice_rules.py from CB_RULES.md; do not edit)
CB_RULES.md is the master and wins. This file holds the rules that touch your job. Read it instead of the whole book. If a rule you need seems missing, grep CB_RULES.md for the word; do not read it top to bottom.

## RULE NO. 1: MAKE A RICK-QUALITY VIDEO. If this fails, everything is wrong.
(CB 2026-11-11: "no1 rule is to make ricks quality video", "if is fails everything is wrong")
- [ ] Every rule below serves this one. Following a workflow step, passing a gate or ticking a box never excuses a result that is below Rick's.
- [ ] THE TEST, on every picture and every clip before CB sees it: put ours next to a Rick frame of the same kind of shot (same shot size, same kind of place). Ask plainly: would this pass as a frame from his channel? Look at story clarity, world detail, light and shadow, reflection, colour, acting, camera.
- [ ] If ours is clearly weaker, it is NOT done. Fix it, or tell CB exactly what is still below Rick and why. Never present it as finished.
- [ ] If a workflow, tool or note leads to a result below Rick, the workflow is wrong: stop, say so, and use the method that reached the quality before (the airfield way).

## HARD RULE NO. 2: NOTHING GENERIC PASSES. EVERYTHING IS ULTRA DETAILED. (CB 2026-11-11: "Can we add rules hard rule. Nothing generic wont pass. Everything need to be ultra detailed")
This is a gate, not advice. A frame that fails it is not shown to CB and not rendered further.
- **Generic = fail.** A plain box, ball tree, flat one-colour surface, typed font, filler word, star in place of a word, empty prop, standing or floor-sit pose where the story needs a real action, or a set that could belong to any film.
- **Every object in frame is specific to THIS story** and built from real parts, down to the small things: a wallet has pockets, stitching, a photo and flies that fly out; a board carries a real blueprint; a cart carries the ride's name; a loop under construction shows the crane and the missing piece.
- **Scale is checked:** trees about a quarter of the hero structure, a vehicle small around its rider, characters as large in frame as Rick's.
- **Poses are specific:** seated means a chair-sit with knees forward, sleeping means slumped with a tilt; body moves come from the trained motion library.
- **The test before CB sees it:** put the frame beside Rick's and name five specific details in every main object. If you cannot, or if Rick's shows a kind of thing ours lacks, it fails. Fix it first.
Full detail list: section 3, "PREMIUM DETAIL IN EVERYTHING".

## 11. THE LEAN PIPELINE AND THE TOKEN RULES (CB 2026-11-15 after the armor film: "how we can optimized that is not burn too much tokes and quicker to make", "or what takes so much time and not worth", then "yes please do."). Wins over every older pipeline line in this file and in SKILL.md.
Why: the armor film (63.5 s) cost 1.66 billion tokens, 41 helpers and 22.7 working hours. Measured: about 750 million went into a still-picture storyboard with judge rounds that CB rejected when he saw it move; 97 % of all tokens were re-reading (every step a helper takes re-reads everything it has seen so far); builder 1 alone cost 184 million because one conversation ran 13 hours. Target for the next film of the same quality: at most 450 million tokens and 12 working hours.

### 11a. The lean pipeline (the order of work)
1. STORY AND VOICE, THEN THE PICTURE PLAN. One story unless CB asks for a choice; facts checked; voice recorded; `words.json`; then `PICTURE_PLAN.md` (11d): what the viewer sees on each word, written for this story.
2. THE ONE GATE: THE WHOLE FILM ROUGH, PLUS THE HOOK MOVING. As soon as script, voice and the first character are locked, one builder per stretch starts at once (section 10) with a cap of 60-90 minutes and brings 2-3 real three.js key frames for EVERY line of its stretch: no polish, stand-in cast allowed. The hook builder also brings its 10-15 s in motion with voice and captions. CB sees the picture plan, the whole board with its line check and the moving hook together, and says yes or no. Nothing is polished and no judge runs before this gate. Why both: the armor film showed that stills cannot prove motion or camera (CB rejected what the stills had passed); the Moonrakers film showed that polishing one scene for a day before CB has seen the whole film wastes the day (CB 2026-11-14: "til now i dint see the storybaord", then "Board all 20 lines now"). This replaces the hook-frame gate of section 0.
3. BUILD OUT AND POLISH THE STRETCHES from the approved board, in parallel (section 10), from ONE shared sets folder from the first day (never a copy of the sets per stretch), with the strong colours already in (11c). CB's approved board is the FLOOR: a polished frame keeps every story element its board panel shows (props, characters, the gag, the named thing) and the light of its chapter; the builder checks board beside polish before reporting.
4. CB'S NOTES IN BATCHES. The lead collects all notes on a version, runs the automatic checks first, then sends ONE fix round per version. Aim: two rounds.
5. SOUND, then THE GRADE as the last picture step, then delivery.
ONE FOLDER PER FILM (CB 2026-11-15: "never create so many subfolder. for one keep same name and create inside subfolder with version"). A film lives in ONE folder, `episodes/<name>/`, named after the film, never after a prompt or a task. Stretches, versions, fixes and tests go INSIDE it: `episodes/<name>/s2/`, `episodes/<name>/v3/`, `episodes/<name>/_tmp/`. Never a sibling folder such as `<name>-s2`, `<name>-s4a-raid`, `_ridefix_tmp_s4a` or `continue-<name>-from-handoff...`. Every helper brief names its subfolder inside the film folder. Temp folders are deleted when their stretch lands. At delivery the film folder keeps the final video, the scripts, the notes and the code; frame folders, old versions and logs are deleted. DELETE DIRECTLY, WITHOUT ASKING, as soon as the final is approved (CB 2026-11-15: "next time please delete directly after everything final keep only neccessary files and final files"): keep the final video(s), scripts, notes, code, cast, refs, sets and sound; delete every frame folder, old version, old animatic, log and temp folder. Then decode the kept final once to prove it plays.
Not in the pipeline any more, used only when CB asks for them by name:
- Department rounds on still pictures BEFORE the gate (camera, light, props and effects each sending fix rounds on a storyboard) and judge loops. On the armor film three such rounds chased judge scores of 5.5 and 6.8 and none of that work reached the film; on Moonrakers six judge and fix rounds went into 7.5 s while 18 lines were not started. A judge runs at most ONCE per version, AFTER the gate, on the moving clip and its sheets; never judge, fix, judge more than twice without CB seeing the version. The lead still LOOKS at the check sheets before CB sees anything (section 7 stays).
- A Blender layer. It cost about 80 million tokens and 6 hours for a gain that is hard to see on a phone. Use it only when a polished, glass or wet hero object is the star of the story, test it on 2 frames first, and put it only where that object covers at least 1.5 % of the picture.
- A repaint of finished sets. Colour is decided before the sets are built (11c).

### 11b. Token rules (every helper and the lead)
- T1 READ ONLY YOUR SLICE. A helper reads `rules/dept/<its department>.md` (made by `python tools/slice_rules.py`) and the files its brief names. It never reads the whole of CB_RULES.md or SKILL.md; when it needs one more rule it greps for the word. Only the lead reads the whole book, once per session.
- T2 A FRESH HELPER FOR EVERY FIX ROUND. A helper does one build or one fix round, then it ends. Before it reports it writes `STATE.md` in its work folder (at most 60 lines): what is built, the files and frame folders, the numbers measured, what is weak, what is open. The next round is a NEW helper that reads STATE.md and the notes. Never resume a helper that already did a round: each resumed step re-reads its whole history. (This replaces "one builder who stays through every fix round" in section 10.)
- T3 NUMBERS BEFORE PICTURES. Anything a script can measure is checked by a script that prints numbers: a figure cut by the frame edge, the named thing in frame on its word, floor share, saturation and brightness, frozen frames, loudness. A helper opens a picture only when a number fails or for the one final look. Pictures are looked at small: one sheet at most 1,600 px wide, at most 4 pictures per check round, never full-size frames one by one.
- T4 ONE COMMAND PER CYCLE. Render, sheets and measurements run from ONE script call. A long run goes in the background and the helper ends its turn; it does not wake up to wait, poll or look at a log. Every wake-up re-reads everything.
- T5 SHORT REPORTS, DETAIL IN FILES. A helper's report is at most 25 lines: done, numbers, weak points, files. Tables and lists go into a file the report names.
- T6 THE SMALL MODEL FOR MECHANICAL WORK. Rendering, joining, measuring, merging, fact checks, sound mix runs and file moves go to a helper on the smaller model (Agent tool `model: sonnet` or `haiku`). The main model is for story, acting, camera and look decisions.
- T7 A FRESH LEAD SESSION PER PHASE. Story, build and finish are three sessions, each started from HANDOFF.md. The lead never reads a helper's transcript and never pastes long tool output into the chat when a file path will do.
- T8 NOTHING BUILT TWICE. Before a helper builds a tool, a set part or a move, it greps `tools/`, `templates/` and the last episode for one that exists. Studies of Rick are done once and live in the rules and `references/`; a film does not study him again unless CB names a new question.
- T9 MEASURE EVERY FILM. At delivery the lead runs `python tools/token_report.py` and writes the totals into HANDOFF.md: tokens per helper, working hours, and the three most expensive helpers with the reason. A helper over 60 million tokens is a fault to explain.

### 11c. Colour from the first day
- The LOOK_BIBLE carries the measured targets before any set is built: saturation of the ungraded frames at least 0.36 for the whole film and 0.30 by day, a clearly different colour world per kind of light (distance between light kinds at least 18 before the grade), night frames never under mean brightness 0.31, one red in the film, faces white by day.
- Sets start from the armor film's coloured values (`episodes/armor-no-holes/colour_pass/COLOUR_PASS.md`: the pigment key `rich`, the light colours per place), not from grey defaults.
- The grade is the last picture step and is cheap (armor: 8 million tokens, 3 minutes for the whole film): start from `episodes/armor-no-holes/grade_final/` (per light kind, with the guards for reds, faces, caption letters and the ceiling).

### 11d. Solve it before it is built (CB 2026-11-15: "i want it have the problem solve in first place not to much fine tune", then "every story is different. it need to match to the story")
Why: of CB's 23 notes on the armor film about 14 were "the thing the voice names is not shown, not close enough or not highlighted", about 5 were "someone is cut off or stands wrong", about 4 were acting or a gag. Almost all were knowable before a frame was built.
- THE PICTURE PLAN, BEFORE ANY BUILD. After the script and voice the writer and the lead write `episodes/<name>/PICTURE_PLAN.md` in the format of `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md`: one row for every thing or action the voice names, with the word it lands on, what we see, CLOSE / IN SCENE / NOT SHOWN and WHY in this story, the character's feeling on that word, an effect or gag only if this story's world gives one. CB approves it with the rough board (the one gate). Every row is a must for the builder; the line-check sheet is ordered by its rows.
- THE STORY DECIDES, NEVER A TEMPLATE. The plan is a format, not content: it is written fresh from each script and no row is copied from another film. A close-up goes in only where it fits the scene (section 10: secondary, must match the scene). "The voice says it" is not a reason; the reason is what the thing does in the story. Rick's numbers (96 % shown on the word, about 40 % close) check the total at the end and are never a quota per line.
- A LIBRARY OF PIECES IS TECHNIQUE, NOT CONTENT. Proven pieces live in `templates/pieces/` (built 2026-11-15 from the armor film: 17 pieces; 12 as code = hop, laugh, hit, double tap, live stroke, "got it", "told you so", the motion helpers, highlight of a part, fly-and-hit, burst of living things, time pass; 5 as numbers only = push-in, low-angle close-up, fly through an object, fly-land-rest, the "hundreds" count). Read `templates/pieces/INDEX.md`: each entry says WHEN IT FITS and when not, and what must change. `node templates/pieces/prove.mjs` and `prove_fx.mjs` must print PASS after any edit there. Known limits: the amounts of lean, arm and head inside a move are still the armor characters' and need an animator for another body; effect files give numbers per frame, the look is built new in the film's set module; the first film that imports a piece tests ONE move through the kit first (`templates/pieces/STATE.md`). A plan row names the piece AND what changes for this story (object, light, character). A piece used unchanged is generic and fails Hard Rule No. 2.
- AUTOMATIC FRAME CHECKS BEFORE CB SEES A VERSION: `node tools/frame_checks/check.mjs <film.json>` (built and proven 2026-11-15; about 40 s per stretch, quarter size, one process). On every camera rest it tests, per character: head with hat cut by the frame edge; the figure cut through by a side edge; set geometry between the camera and the face, or the head inside a mesh; feet floating or sunk. It prints numbers, saves one small crop per FAIL and exits 1 on a FAIL. Every builder runs it before reporting, and the lead before CB sees a version. A version with a FAIL is not sent, unless the picture-plan row says in words that the figure at the edge is meant (a CLOSE on a thing with a face at the edge); such a waiver is named in the report. Proof: it caught three planted faults (head cut 23 %, body cut 49 %, head inside the engine) and found the Chief's face cut in half at the edge of the chalk close-up in the approved armor film (S1 frames 184-205), which nobody had seen. Limits: three.js stage only, not a Blender pass; one character covering another is not reported; a moving character is exempt on that frame; tuned on two stretches of one film.
- A NOTE FROM CB IS CHECKED AGAINST THE PLAN. Was the row there? If not, the row is added to the film's plan, and if the kind of thing was missing from the format, `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md` gets the line, so the next film's plan catches it.

## 8. Build fixes learned (magic bell, 2026-11-11). Each one cost a re-render; check them before rendering
- [ ] Run `proj.py tune.json` before EVERY render: each card's feet and head must land inside 0.08..0.92 of the frame width, and the camera must not sit inside any set object (booth radius, candle stands, walls). A camera inside geometry gives a black or curtain-only frame.
- [ ] Black things need a light background: black palms, ink, a dark thief. Put them in front of a bright doorway, window, moon or plain warm wall, never in front of a black curtain or a night sky. If the set has nothing bright behind, build it (front wall + lit doorway, moon disc).
- [ ] A reverse shot needs the 4th wall built. Never point the camera at an open side of the set (empty sky in an interior = generic = fail).
- [ ] Group rows: space cards so raised hands do not cover a neighbour's face (about 0.95 m apart for arms-up poses, wider lens), and check no face is cut by the frame edge.
- [ ] Hands on an object: cards turn toward the camera, so place the card origin at hand point minus the hand offset (from cards/meta.json) along screen-right, with the hand a few cm in front of the surface facing the camera; otherwise the hand sinks behind the object.
- [ ] Held props are drawn AT the hand in the card (P.held svg): palms, ink brush, chest, cookie. Never a separate floating prop.
- [ ] A backdrop plane behind a window (sky, garden) must not cast shadows (visible_shadow = False), or the sun patch through the window disappears.
- [ ] Night look: deep readable blue sky (not black), cool moon key, warm lanterns, a silhouette against a big moon disc for the hook of a night beat.
- [ ] Props that prove the story are built in 3D with their marks: the ink bell = glossy black body, four bronze handprints wiped out of the ink (palm + 4 fingers + thumb), drips at the lip.
- [ ] Cloud bpy needs `apt-get install libegl1 libegl-mesa0`, or bpy dies silently with exit 134.
- [ ] Dark limbs vanish on dark objects (ink-black arm on the black ink bell): draw a white open palm at the hand (cards_gen over.palmHand) so every touch reads. Place a touch card WITHOUT the mirror flag (mirror puts the hand on the other side).
- [ ] Cloud renders die when the container idles: render each still in the foreground (res 55, 20 samples, about 8 min) and send results as they finish.
- [ ] Card lighting in Blender (2026-11-12): the card shader takes light from both faces (diffuse + translucent) with an own-colour floor of 0.7 by day and 0.35 at night, plus a key-side band: the half toward the key is brighter in the key colour, the far half takes a cool shadow tint (hall_head.py card(), tune card_emit, card_side, card_band). Do not stack edge_shadow.py on v12+ cards: the template draws the face shadow.
- [ ] Rick 6b colour pass (softer, brighter world, haze lifts the darkest tones): keep a black hero object black. Protect pixels darker than about 0.09 by about 75 % so the ink bell or any black hero prop stays glossy black, and keep the cast on its own layer on top (magic bell post6b.py, 'ink' mode).
- [ ] MECHANICS, BANNERS, EFFECTS (roller coaster round 2, CB's notes 2026-11-13 01:50 Bangkok: "summerize what you learn from this ... remember the camera movement"; full text project files episodes/roller-coaster/final/LESSONS_round2_2026-11-13.md): 1 cranks and handles turn with the fists ON the grip every frame: measure the fists per frame and drive the crank angle from that. 2 Banners hang still (stretched canvas on battens, no wind or folds); letters painted into the cloth material, never a see-through plane in front of a close character; nothing hangs in front of the words. 3 Mechanical motion follows the sound: a part that clicks 3 times moves in 3 steps with a small overshoot, never one smooth bend; when a part changes shape, hide every other version of it. 4 A person in a vehicle sits inside it: whole face in the windscreen, head under the roof; check the close shot. 5 Highlights on metal travel: they spread outward along the rail and slide, never sit still. 6 No effect freezes before the last frame: explosions keep growing and throwing bits to the end. 7 Wood reads as wood: grain along each part, knots, warm brown.
- [ ] FIREWORKS CREW TEST FIXES (2026-11-13, thread "Test crew with fireworks shot"; notes in project files episodes/fireworks-test crew/LEAD_QUEUE.md, look/LOOK_LOG.md, look/hybrid_v1/README.md): 1 render --animatic muxes the voice with -shortest, which cut a 21.2 s film to 20.13 s: pad the audio to the film length (or drop -shortest) and check the final duration. 2 Parallel department renders must each write their own stills folder (render.mjs --stills-dir <dir>, in the fireworks kit_patch until the master has it); a shared out/stills lost the judge's frames twice. 3 Long renders are resumable (frame-skip by existing file, chunks, a log), because a container restart kills untracked jobs. 4 Blender layers: glints on snow work; a bounce-light layer needs the sky key off and a character mask, or it veils the snow and greys the cards; lantern glow went neon and volumetric smoke flattened the sky, so drop those layers unless a before/after proves them. 5 The lock export writes decal alpha as white (snow footprints): dump decals separately (look/dump_decals.mjs) before a Blender layer pass.

## RULES FROM OTHER SECTIONS THAT NAME YOUR SUBJECT
### from 0. How to work (before anything is built)
- [ ] Need CB's OK: any online/RunPod render, changes to the locked cast or MAIN LOOK. One Blender job at a time.



### from 3. World and look (Rick's 3D world, never a flat drawing)
- [ ] The WORLD is real 3D with real materials, light, shadow and reflection. Only the characters are flat 2D cards. A flat 2D drawing of the whole scene is wrong. ("oh no. what are you doing that is not like ricks")
- [ ] HOW THE WORLD IS MADE, never skipped (CB 2026-11-11: "make image in code first and we can compare", "and then put in blender", "totally different from the witch and airfield"; CB also corrected the skipping of Stage 1 twice on 2026-11-09):
  1. Hero object first, alone, as a detailed model (airfield: the Po-2, about 38,000 triangles; BlenderKit first).
  2. STAGE 1 = the picture made in code: the whole scene built by Python as a dense 3D scene in the finished toon-and-ink look (30+ prop kinds, 600+ objects, one clear focal point, lamps, haze), with render-look-fix rounds until it matches references/look_locked/stage1_airfield_approved.png in quality. Show CB.
  3. STAGE 2 = Blender material effects: the SAME scene converted to the locked main look (materials, engine light, grade). Nothing rebuilt. Target: night_airfield_approved.png.
  CB'S 7 BUILD STEPS, in this order for every place (CB 2026-11-11: "1. shot plan, 2. then the build, 3. then check camera angle, 4. environment overhaul, 5 post procession, 6 shading, 7 check the frames send fix to builder"):
  1. Shot plan: shot table row + Rick reference frames for this shot, before any model.
  2. Build: hero object alone, then the scene blocks and the characters in library poses.
  3. Camera check: lens, height and angle against the Rick frame of the same shot kind; subject big, hero object not covered, faces above the caption line. Fix the camera BEFORE adding detail.
  4. Environment overhaul: Stage 1 density (30+ prop kinds, 600+ objects, big foreground props, background, sky).
  5. Post processing: grade and bloom (post_toon.py, later grade.py).
  6. Shading: Stage 2 = Blender LAYERS only over the coded frame (see BLENDER = ONLY THE LAYERS IT DOES BETTER).
  7. Check the frames: a SEPARATE checker (not the builder) looks at every frame beside the Rick frame and the look_locked target, writes one fix list, the builder fixes all, repeat until it passes. Only then CB sees it.
  ADDED TO THE 7 STEPS (proposed by Claude 2026-11-11 after CB asked "what else we need?"; CB can strike any of them):
  a. Before step 1, the ONE-LINE PICTURE TEST: write in one sentence what the viewer understands with the sound off. No sentence = no shot.
  b. Inside step 2, ACTING: poses from the motion library, hands ending on the object, calm start face. Checked before the camera.
  c. Between 4 and 5, LIGHT as its own step: one key light, hard long shadows on the floor, the subject brighter than the background.
  d. Shading (6) is judged before the final grade; post processing is run again last, on the shaded frame.
  e. After 7, MOTION CHECK: the shot is checked moving (walk, push-in, the way in and out of the shot), not only as a still.
  f. A frame CB approves is saved to references/look_locked as the new target for the next episodes.
  The three.js scene is for staging, camera and timing only. A flat sketch or a simple block set is never shown as the look. Details: SKILL.md FULL WORKFLOW steps 4-7, memory airfield-process.md.
- [ ] LIGHT AND BRIGHTNESS ARE FINISHED IN THE CODED STORYBOARD; BLENDER KEEPS THEM (CB 2026-11-11 on the dark night station test: "why is ours so dark and bad lighting", "contrast is too strong", "light brightness should be finished in the coded already. The Blender just gives the effects and material and texture, but keep the coded style"). Blender adds materials, textures, real shadows, reflections and effects only. Before CB sees a Blender frame, put it next to the coded frame of the same moment: overall brightness, how even the light is, and each surface's colour must match the coded one. Never one strong spotlight that leaves the rest dark, never crushed blacks, no added contrast or dark corners in the finishing step. Night = an evenly lit scene tinted blue (as Rick does), not a dark scene with a lamp.
- [ ] BLENDER = ONLY THE LAYERS IT DOES BETTER (CB 2026-11-13 10:48 Bangkok, roller coaster thread: "yes thats the new rule. only take what blender do better."). For every film the coded three.js frame is the FINAL BASE: faces, cards, colours, light, framing and fx stay exactly as they are. A full Blender frame is no longer the final picture. Blender renders only MASKED LAYERS from the same lock camera, composited over the coded frame: metal reflections that move with the camera, wood grain and surface texture, bounce light, lit smoke and haze, light glowing through paper or snow, glints, motion blur on fast fx (never on characters). Each layer gets a before/after against the coded frame shown to CB; keep only a layer that clearly adds something, never one that makes the frame darker or flatter. This REPLACES the old Stage 2 "whole frame in Blender" step (step 6 above and SKILL.md FULL WORKFLOW Stage B are now "Blender layers"); BLENDER KEEPS THE CODED LIGHT and BLENDER NEVER WEAKER still hold. First used on the fireworks test (snow sparkle and burst bounce kept; lanterns, smoke and blur dropped).
- [ ] BLENDER NEVER WEAKER THAN THE STORYBOARD (CB 2026-11-12 10:11Z on the roller coaster Blender film: "Is almost a downgrade", "texture details FX lighting missing", "no hammer, no blueprint chart, no money pocket"). A Blender frame is never weaker than its storyboard frame. Before CB sees any Blender picture, every frame (every 0.5 s) is put beside its storyboard frame; any prop, painted texture, glow or light pool, colour, or word that the storyboard has and the Blender frame lacks means the frame is not done. Things the lock export loses and must be carried over: held props (unnamed meshes in noExport groups), canvas-painted faces (boards, plates, patterned cloth), sky details (moon craters, night clouds), objects hidden at frame 0 (crash parts), instanced part colours (instances.json base), vertex-painted ground colours, and painted word planes, which must be parented to the cloth they hang on. No sheen on grass or leaves, because it turns lawns pale.
- [ ] PRODUCTION-READY 3D MATERIALS, MECHANICAL GEOMETRY AND BLENDER SHADING (CB 2026-11-13 02:09 Bangkok, pasted as a rule; his 16 points kept): identify the correct real-world materials, construction, surface properties and mechanical relationships for every object in the story. 1 MATERIAL IDENTIFICATION: name each component's material (wood, metal, stone, concrete, glass, plastic, rubber, fabric, soil, grass, water...) and give it a matching shader; never generic plastic-looking materials. 2 CLEAN MODELING: correct scale, consistent topology, real thickness, correct normals, clean intersections, subtle edge bevels; no holes, overlapping faces, z-fighting, broken surfaces or needless polygons. 3 MECHANICAL PLAUSIBILITY: tools, machines, furniture, vehicles and structures have parts that could work: hinges on valid pivots, wheels on axles, screws and bolts joining parts, gears that mesh, supports that carry the load, clearance for moving parts; no decorative mechanics that cannot function. 4 PBR MATERIALS: base colour, roughness, metallic, normal or bump, and displacement or transmission where needed; reflectance and finish match the real material. 5 WOOD: grain direction follows the shape and how the part was made, end grain on cross cuts, fibre variation, believable cut faces, knots where they fit. 6 METAL: polished, brushed, painted, rusty and rough metal look different (metallic response, reflection, roughness, wear, machining detail). 7 STONE AND CONCRETE: irregular surfaces, chips, pores, cracks, layers, roughness; natural rock, cut stone and concrete look different. 8 GRASS AND VEGETATION: grounded blades or clumps with natural size and direction variation, density that fits, real transitions to other ground; no flat plastic grass, no repeating pattern. 9 GLASS AND TRANSPARENT: real thickness, transmission, refraction, reflection, roughness; clear glass, frosted glass and plastic look different. 10 SHINE: highlights and reflections come from material, light and geometry (roughness, reflectivity, environment), never painted white glare. 11 UV AND TEXTURE: consistent texture scale and texel density, logical UV direction, minimal stretching, deliberate or seamless material transitions. 12 STYLIZED ART DIRECTION: keep our polished stylized 3D cartoon look: clean silhouettes, simplified geometry, readable materials, controlled highlights; no photoreal noise. 13 BLENDER-READY: meshes, materials, textures, pivots, modifiers and object names organised for reuse; editable node materials on Principled BSDF. 14 SURFACE RESPONSE: wood, metal, glass and stone react differently to the same light; forms stay readable with the key light, fill, rim and contact shadows. 15 ASSET CONTINUITY: material identity, texture scale, wear, geometry and mechanics stay the same across all scenes and camera angles. 16 QUALITY VALIDATION before final render: check every asset for wrong materials, stretched textures, too much shine, bad normals, floating parts, intersecting geometry, implausible construction and wrong scale. Every object is recognisable, mechanically understandable where relevant, beautifully shaded and ready for reuse and animation in Blender. HOW IT FITS OUR RULES: point 12's 'consistent outline thickness' means our existing lines only (the cast's outline and fine BUILD lines on objects); no ink outlines on the world (section 3 lines rule stands). Point 14's light stays the coded light (BLENDER KEEPS THE CODED LIGHT: Blender adds no new key or contrast). Characters keep the clean look (CAUTION ON CHARACTERS). Owners: props-hero builds parts and mechanics (point 3) in the kit, 3d-designer owns points 1-2 and 4-13 and 15-16 in Blender with a materials list per object in `look/<place>_MATERIALS.md`, look-finisher and lighting-director check point 14 and 16 on the render.
- [ ] BlenderKit first for hero objects. Renders local EEVEE.


### from 4. Characters
- [ ] Only the locked 2D vector cast, four locked views. Flat cards, no soft 3D bodies.
- [ ] Heads pure WHITE in the finished Blender frame, never grey: the head is fully self-lit (card_emit 1.0, gain 1.3; measured face white 245+ of 255; CB asked twice), the scene light must not dim it. ### from 5. Movement and acting
- [ ] EVERY ACTION IS A MOVE, DRAWN NEW ON EVERY FRAME (CB 2026-11-13 evening "yes make it as rule"; found in the fireworks test lock, where the boy has 636 drawings for 636 frames and every one belongs to a move: kneel, pocket, flick, light, take, brave, flee, lookup, rise, home). How it is built, for every film: 1 film.json sets `"tween": { "ones": true }`. 2 Each action of each character in the script is written as its own EPISODE MOVE (`m:<name>`, a time-driven move function in the motion-library form, played by the kit's motion-library bridge in `templates/threejs_film/puppets.mjs`), built as a STUDIO MOTION action sequence, so the body animates itself through the whole action. 3 Faces come from `faces_ep` and change on the words INSIDE the move. 4 Hands follow per-frame targets on the real prop anchors (`hand_at`, `held3d`). 5 Walks, climbs, kneels and carries come from the trained library. 6 Small living things (a cat, a bird) get their own short pose sequences. A film whose acts are plain poses is not staged yet. CHECK before any storyboard: per character, drawings per second in the lock or the baked performance (the fireworks boy: 30 a second while he acts; the bomber armor animatic: frozen poses with a 7-frame blend).

### from 6b. RICK REFERENCE LESSONS (2026-11-11, thread "Learn from Rick's Clips reference videos";
- [ ] LIGHT FOLLOWS THE STORY CLOCK: when story time passes, the light changes (cart film: day, pink dusk, rain night with lanterns, sunrise, bright day = 5 lights in 67 s). Plan the lights in the shot table; one light for a whole film only if the story really is one moment.

### from 7. Before sending to CB (sign every line by looking, not by the gate report)
- [ ] SHOT-BY-SHOT VISUAL QA LOOP, 12 SCORES (CB 2026-11-13: "create the scene, render a preview, inspect the actual image, identify visible errors, and revise"): every shot is rendered and looked at, never judged from code. The storyboard-judge scores it 1-10 from visible evidence beside the reference in 12 categories: story accuracy, camera and framing, depth, environment richness, modeling detail, materials, lighting, character acting, physical grounding, VFX structure, colour grade, continuity. Any important category under 8 = revise before the next step. Never claim an improvement without rendering and inspecting it, and say plainly what is still below the reference. These scores go on the PROOF PAGE.

### from 9. LESSONS MERGED FROM THE SIDE NOTES (audit 2026-11-13; CB: "everything we learnd from th
- [ ] ANIMATICS ARE RENDERED AT FULL SIZE (CB 2026-11-11 17:03Z, roller coaster: "character need to be sharp everytime he is in the frame"). The soft characters came from a half-size animatic scaled up. Render every animatic CB sees with `render.mjs --animatic --scale 1` (1080x1920).

### from 10. THE PROVEN BUILD METHOD (pin stretch test, CB 2026-11-14: "Yes, rebuild film". Proof: 
- Sheets made for every render and looked at by the builder AND the lead before CB: a strip at 4 frames per second, the LINE CHECK (each line's words beside its frames: do I see what it says?), feet and eyes zooms, a phone-size sheet.
- Renders: full-size frames in parallel chunks (`episodes/armor-no-holes/stretches/armor-pins-test/render_final.sh` is the pattern). With several builders on one PC, at most 3 render processes per builder.
- RENDER ON THE GRAPHICS CARD (CB 2026-11-14: "Can you not use gpu all work?"). `templates/threejs_film/render_gpu.mjs` draws the three.js frames on the RTX 2070 SUPER: about 0.55-0.9 s per full-size frame against 4.7 s in software, picture equal apart from antialiased edges (tested on one film; `GPU_RENDER.md`). One process normally, two only when the card is free, never three, never while Blender uses the card. Never mix software and GPU frames inside one stretch. Check one frame per place both ways before a full run. Why the first try was black: a `pow()` of a slightly negative number in a set shader gives not-a-number on the card, and the bloom blur spread it; any new set shader must guard `pow`, `sqrt` and divisions.
- BLENDER LAYERS ON RUNPOD (CB 2026-11-14: "ok do runpod"). Blender layer frames render on rented RTX 4090 machines, not on our card: the picture matches local to 0.005 of 255, so cloud and local frames can share a shot. One Blender process is held up by the processor (tens of thousands of objects set per frame), so the speed comes from 6-8 processes per machine (4.2-4.6 s a frame against 23 s here) and from several machines at once. Steps and image in `episodes/armor-no-holes/blender_metal/RUNPOD.md` (needs `libegl1 libgl1 libopengl0`). Only the lead creates machines; check a machine's upload speed in the first 2 minutes and drop a slow one (one upload crawled at 18 MB in 20 minutes); terminate each machine the moment its frames are counted on this PC. Armor film: 362 metal frames, about 1 h 20 min of machine time, about 1.30 USD. Put the Blender layer only where the thing it improves covers at least 1.5 % of the picture (measured per frame on the matte); in wide shots it adds glints and nothing to see.
